slides.title: From LLM to agent
slides.subtitle: By this evening: a bounded core loop and three working reasoning agents on Tawseel's order-tracking task.
slides.notes: Point back to the golden-thread slide from the front section and land on the Day 1 row. Say the deliverable out loud so the room knows what 'done' looks like by 5pm: a compiling core loop, plus ReAct, Plan-and-Execute and Reflection all running on the same order-tracking task. Nothing here is throwaway.

slides.title: Agentic system architectures and components
slides.subtitle: The mental model and the minimal working skeleton every later module extends.
slides.notes: This module is the foundation for the whole week: everything else hangs off the loop built here. Say plainly that there are no tools and no memory yet — those are Modules 3 and 4. Today is only the skeleton, on purpose.

slides.title: Structure now is cheaper than an incident later
slides.intro: The shift from answering to acting is why architecture — not prompting — is the precondition for every guardrail that follows.

bullets.text: Saudi enterprises are moving to agents that complete transactions: reschedule a delivery, open a case, reconcile an invoice.
An operator replaces a rules-based IVR with an agent that plans multi-step resolutions, cutting average handle time.
An operations agent gathers evidence from three systems before a human decides — the risk team signs off on the transparency of steps.
A citizen-service agent routes requests across departments; each step is logged as a discrete, reviewable transition.
Explicit state, bounded loops, observable steps are what every guardrail, audit and cost control that follows depends on.

aside.title: THE STAKES
aside.body: An agent that can do things can also do the wrong things at scale, spend money, and touch personal data under PDPL. A well-structured agent is auditable; a while-loop-around-a-prompt is a liability.

slides.notes: Ask the room: has anyone's org shipped something closer to a rules-based IVR wearing an 'AI' label than a real agent? That gap is exactly what this module fixes. Keep this to five minutes — the failure story is coming.

slides.title: LLM call, chain, agent: three control flows
slides.caption: Control flow moves from fixed at authoring time (chain) to decided at runtime by the model (agent) — that runtime choice is the whole point, and the whole risk.
slides.notes: Draw this as three widening boxes on the board first, then reveal the slide. Stress that a RAG pipeline is a chain, not an agent — the LLM fills slots but never chooses the path. Ask which of the room's 'agent' demos are secretly chains wearing an agent's name.

slides.title: The four agentic components

cards.title: Planning
cards.body: What is my approach to the whole task? Decompose 'my order is late, I want a refund' into locate → check SLA → determine eligibility → act.

cards.title: Reasoning
cards.body: What is the single next step, given what I know now? Decide whether to call track_shipment or ask for an order id.

cards.title: Tool use
cards.body: How do I affect or observe the world? Call Tawseel's Order-Management, Logistics-Tracking and CRM APIs via MCP (Module 3).

cards.title: Memory
cards.body: What do I carry within and across tasks? Thread state in a conversation; customer history and policy across sessions (Module 4).

slides.notes: These are roles, not necessarily separate LLM calls — say that explicitly. A ReAct agent fuses planning and reasoning into one stream; Plan-and-Execute separates them (next module). Point at each card and name where it deepens later in the week.

slides.title: An agent is a state machine — build it as one
slides.caption: LangGraph models exactly this: a typed state every node reads and writes, nodes as pure-ish functions, and a conditional edge where agency lives.
slides.notes: This is the engineering insight of the whole module. Write 'State / Nodes / Edges / Termination' on the board and let the class fill in what each means before revealing. Say explicitly: an agent without a guaranteed path to END is a bill waiting to happen.

slides.title: Lab 1's buildable target
slides.caption: This is the whole of build_graph() — no tools yet (Module 3), no memory yet (Module 4). RafeeqState carries messages, customer_id, locale, order_id, step_count, resolution.
slides.notes: This is literally what participants compile in the next 50 minutes. Walk the arrows left to right, then point out there is exactly one conditional edge — that is where all the agency in this graph lives, and it is the only thing Lab 1 asks them to get right.

slides.title: Termination is designed, not hoped for
slides.intro: Three conditions to make explicit and testable — 'the model decides when it's done' is not one of them.

bullets.text: The model emits a final answer with no tool call.
A tool fails after retries — surface it into state, do not loop on it.
Any of the three axes trips — escalate, do not keep asking.
'The model will decide when it's done' is not a termination condition — it is the absence of one.

slides.notes: Read the last bullet aloud, word for word — it is the module's most quoted line. Ask the room to predict, before you reveal graph.py two slides from now, exactly what route() must check to satisfy all three of the first bullets.

slides.title: Four principles to teach explicitly

cards.title: State is the contract
cards.body: Everything a node needs lives in the state object; nodes never reach into globals or hidden context. Testable, checkpointable, inspectable.

cards.title: Bounded by construction
cards.body: Step, cost and time budgets are set when the graph is compiled, not hoped for at runtime.

cards.title: One reason to loop
cards.body: Each iteration must make measurable progress. Re-asking the same question with the same state is an infinite-loop bug.

cards.title: Separate loop from work
cards.body: The graph structure (control) is separate from tool implementations (work) — it pays off in testing (Module 7).

slides.notes: These four sit underneath everything the course does — refer back to them by number in later modules ('this is principle 2 again') rather than re-explaining. Ask pairs which principle broken_agent.py violates hardest; most will say all four.

slides.title: Message list vs typed state

items.text: Nothing to route on — every decision is a guess.
No step_count, no resolution flag.
An auditor cannot answer 'why did it do that?'
messages, customer_id, locale, order_id, step_count, resolution.
route() reads step_count and tool_calls — no guessing.
Every routing decision is derivable from state, on review.

slides.notes: This is mistake #2 from the common-mistakes list, made concrete before you reach that slide. Ask: which side could you unit-test without a running model? Only the right side — that is the whole argument for typed state in one question.

slides.title: Version everything that shapes behaviour

bullets.text: Version the graph definition by git SHA — a routing change is a diff, not a mystery.
Version the model name, parameters and prompt templates alongside it.
A tool's input/output shape is part of the contract — version it too.
A synchronous API call and an offline batch replay over historical tickets should drive the SAME compiled graph.

slides.notes: The batch-replay point is the seed of the whole evaluation harness the course builds toward — flag that explicitly. If both entry points drive the same compiled graph, the architecture is right; if replay needs its own copy of the logic, something in the design has already gone wrong.

slides.title: Chain or agent?
slides.intro: No lecture — sort scenario cards onto the chain↔agent spectrum and defend the boundary cases.
bullets: Translate a document — chain: the steps never change.
Reschedule a delivery — mostly chain, the steps are known.
Negotiate an open-ended refund dispute — agent: the path is discovered.

bullets.text: Rafeeq's 'track my order' flow — where would you put it, and why?

slides.notes: This is the package's fourteen-card sort, condensed to five prompts for a 50-minute lab morning. Run it as a quick show-of-hands per card rather than a full sort if you are short on time; the boundary-case discussion is worth more than the sorting itself.

slides.title: ANTI-PATTERN — the runaway agent
slides.code:
# ANTI-PATTERN: unbounded loop, no termination condition
from rafeeq.core.llm import get_model

CONFUSED_CUSTOMER_MESSAGE = "مش عارف, بس ساعدني لو سمحت"

def run_forever() -> None:
    model = get_model()
    # SMELL: state is a bare, untyped list — nothing to route on
    messages: list[tuple[str, str]] = [("human", CONFUSED_CUSTOMER_MESSAGE)]
    call_count = 0
    # SMELL: no step budget, no cost cap, no wall-clock timeout
    while True:
        reply = model.invoke(messages)
        call_count += 1
        print(f"[call {call_count:>4}] model says: {reply.content!r}")
        # SMELL: the model's own "done" signal is read nowhere
        messages = messages  # nothing about the turn ever advances

callouts.text: while True with nothing bounding steps, cost or wall-clock time — mistake #1.
A bare message list can't be routed on or asserted against — mistake #2.
The final-answer / no-tool-call signal is never read — 'the model decides' isn't even wired up.

slides.notes: Run this live if you have not already burned the tokens on the earlier walkthrough. Let the call counter climb past 20 before killing it with Ctrl-C. Then point at each # SMELL comment and name which of the six common mistakes it is.

slides.title: The fix: reason and route
slides.code:
from rafeeq.core.config import MAX_STEPS
from rafeeq.core.state import RafeeqState
from rafeeq.core.llm import get_model

def reason(state: RafeeqState) -> dict:
    model = get_model()
    reply = model.invoke([SYSTEM, *state["messages"]])
    return {"messages": [reply], "step_count": state["step_count"] + 1}

def route(state: RafeeqState) -> str:
    # TEACHING POINT: bounded by construction, checked in code
    if state["step_count"] >= MAX_STEPS:      # step budget exhausted
        return END
    last = state["messages"][-1]
    if getattr(last, "tool_calls", None):     # wants to act -> loop
        return "reason"
    return END                                # final answer

def build_graph():
    g = StateGraph(RafeeqState)
    g.add_node("reason", reason)
    g.add_edge(START, "reason")
    g.add_conditional_edges("reason", route)  # agency lives here
    return g.compile()

callouts.text: step_count >= MAX_STEPS returns END before the model gets another turn. MAX_STEPS is 8, from config, never re-declared.
No pending tool call also returns END — both paths reach END, so route can never loop forever.
add_conditional_edges is the one place the model's decision changes control flow; everything else is fixed.

slides.notes: This is the real file, trimmed only for the slide — nothing here is paraphrased. Walk both branches of route() before you show build_graph(): 'both branches reach END' is the one sentence that fixes broken_agent.py, said out loud.

slides.statement: Bound the loop, type the state, and every later guardrail has somewhere to attach.

slides.notes: Say it, pause, let it land. Everything from Module 3's tool schemas to Module 8's guardrails to Module 9's tracing attaches to the state object and the graph structure built today — this sentence is why the week does not need to rebuild the core loop again.

slides.title: Six mistakes the Lab 1 starter hides on purpose

bullets.text: while True around a chat call — the canonical runaway agent.
An ever-growing raw message list — impossible to route on or assert against.
The agent can only stop by erroring or exhausting the context window.
'Refunds over 500 SAR need approval' baked into the system prompt, not graph structure — fixed in Module 7.
Tool errors caught and ignored, so the loop continues on stale or empty observations.
Treated as one function — no way to inspect why it chose a step.

slides.notes: Each of these appears deliberately in the Lab 1 starter repo — this is not a hypothetical list. Have the room match each mistake to the # SMELL comments they already found in broken_agent.py before you move to the case study.

slides.title: Case study: the runaway refund agent
slides.scenario: SahlPay, a regional payments and marketplace player, shipped an autonomous refund assistant built as a while loop over a chat model with a 'you may call these tools' system prompt. It demoed beautifully to executives. Support handles roughly 18,000 contacts a day; even a 0.5% error rate is 90 mishandled money movements daily.
slides.challenge: Within two weeks: double refunds, because the loop re-entered the refund branch after an unobserved tool timeout. Runaway runs — one confused customer triggered 140 model calls. Zero auditability: 'why did it refund twice?' had no answer, because there were no discrete steps to inspect.
slides.solution: Re-cast as a bounded state machine: typed state with an explicit refund_issued flag so the branch is entered at most once; step, cost and time budgets with escalation on exhaustion; every transition logged as a discrete, replayable event; tool errors surfaced into state, never swallowed. No new model, no new tools — only architecture.
questions: Which single architectural change prevents the double refund, and why does a better prompt not?
What must a per-transition audit log contain to satisfy a financial regulator?
The CEO wants 'more autonomy' — where would you add structure instead, and how do you sell that as safer and cheaper?
slides.notes: Facilitate, do not lecture — this is a discussion case, not a reveal. Push on question 3 especially: the sellable answer is that structure is what makes MORE autonomy possible later, not what blocks it now. Ten minutes, cap it.

slides.title: Planning and reasoning patterns
slides.subtitle: ReAct, Plan-and-Execute and Reflection — the same Tawseel task, three shapes of thought, one 20x cost lever.
slides.notes: The Module 1 loop from this morning is empty scaffolding until something decides HOW to think — that is this module's whole argument. Say up front that Lab 2 spans two 50-minute blocks; do not compress the build time to make room for slides.

slides.title: Pattern choice is the biggest lever you have
slides.intro: The reasoning pattern is the single biggest lever on an agent's cost and reliability — bigger than model choice.

bullets.text: Flexible, but it can wander and rack up token bills.
Cheaper and predictable for known workflows, brittle when reality diverges from the plan.
Buys quality at a latency and cost premium.
Choosing wrongly turns a 0.02 SAR contact into a 0.40 SAR contact — invisible in a demo, fatal at 18,000 contacts a day.

aside.title: REGULATED SAUDI CONTEXTS
aside.body: Plan-and-Execute also offers an inspectable plan a human can approve before any action runs — the plan itself is a control point, not just a cost saver.

slides.notes: Ask the room to guess, before you show any numbers, how big the cost spread between patterns could be for the same task. Most will guess 2-3x. The 20x figure from the front section's intro is the same number this module measures directly.

slides.title: ReAct: reasoning and acting interleaved

cards.title: What it is
cards.body: Thought → action → observation, repeated in one interleaved stream until the model answers with no further tool call.

cards.title: Strength
cards.body: Flexibility — the path is discovered as information arrives; ideal when the resolution is genuinely unknown.

cards.title: Weakness
cards.body: Can wander and repeat itself; every step re-sends the growing history, so cost grows super-linearly.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Thrashing, premature answering, context bloat — history so long the model loses the goal.

slides.notes: In LangGraph terms this is exactly the Module 1 loop with a tools node: reason ⇄ tools until no tool call remains. Say that connection explicitly before moving to the next card set — it is why Lab 2's ReAct implementation feels familiar.

slides.title: Plan-and-Execute: decide first, then act

cards.title: What it is
cards.body: A planner produces an ordered list of sub-tasks; an executor carries out each one, usually with a cheaper model or a fixed tool call.

cards.title: Strength
cards.body: Predictability and cost — the expensive planning happens once, and the plan is an inspectable artefact a human can approve.

cards.title: Weakness
cards.body: Brittle: a plan built on incomplete information marches confidently in the wrong direction without a replan step.

cards.label: fit
cards.title: Enterprise fit
cards.body: Known, repeatable workflows — refund processing, delivery reschedule — where human approval of the plan is valuable.

slides.notes: Stress 'inspectable artefact' — that word does real work in regulated contexts. Preview that the plan is logged before any step executes in the code you show in a few slides; that ordering is the enterprise argument, not an implementation detail.

slides.title: Reflection: critique before returning

cards.title: What it is
cards.body: After a candidate answer, a critic pass checks it against explicit criteria and revises if needed — self- or external critic.

cards.title: Strength
cards.body: Quality — catches confident-but-wrong outputs before the customer sees them; the critique is auditable.

cards.title: Weakness
cards.body: Cost and latency — at least one extra round-trip per pass; the loop must itself be bounded.

cards.label: rule
cards.title: Placement rule
cards.body: Reflect on high-stakes, hard-to-reverse outputs — money, compliance — not on every 'where is my order' answer.

slides.notes: The placement rule card is the one participants forget by Lab 2 — some pairs will reflexively add Reflection everywhere because it 'sounds safer'. Flag now that the code-review exercise later this module is built entirely around catching that mistake.

slides.title: Why we build ReAct by hand first

bullets.text: ReAct — 'Reason + Act' — interleaves reasoning and acting in one stream, the paper's own framing and the default agentic pattern.
react_loop_explicit() runs thought → action → observation by hand, against plain *_impl tools — no ToolNode, no bind_tools magic.
Only once the loop's shape is boring and obvious should Module 3+'s ToolNode feel like a convenience, not a magic trick.
count_redundant_tool_calls scores every trace: the same tool called with the same args twice is thrashing, made visible.

slides.notes: Name the paper on the slide, out loud: Yao et al. Do not invent a citation year you have not checked — 'Yao et al.' is enough. Show react_loop_explicit()'s printed Thought/Action/Observation trace lines live if the room's energy can take one more demo.

This course teaches the reasoning patterns; the framework only abstracts them. You built ReAct by hand before you ever called bind_tools.
Good for anyone who wants more LangGraph surface area than five days can cover — streaming, subgraphs, human-in-the-loop primitives.
It teaches the library. It does not teach when Plan-and-Execute beats ReAct on a Tawseel refund — that judgement is this course's job.

slides.notes: A team built a 'smart' support agent entirely in ReAct — brilliant in the demo. Narrate: every routine contact ran 4-7 reasoning steps, each re-sending a bloated history. Refactoring the routine 80% to a 2-step Plan-and-Execute flow cut cost about 90% and improved latency; the open-ended 20% kept ReAct. Four minutes, no slide detail beyond these numbers.

slides.title: ReAct, built by hand
slides.code:
def react_loop_explicit(objective: str, *, max_steps=MAX_STEPS,
                         tool_impls=None, verbose=True) -> ReactTrace:
    """Thought -> action -> observation, by hand. No ToolNode."""
    impls = tool_impls or _default_tool_impls()
    messages = [("human", objective)]
    trace = ReactTrace(objective=objective)
    for step_no in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        model = get_model().bind_tools([{"name": n} for n in impls])
        reply = model.invoke([("system", REACT_SYSTEM_TEXT), *messages])
        if not reply.tool_calls:
            trace.final_answer = reply.content
            trace.terminated_reason = "final_answer"
            return _finalise(trace)
        call = reply.tool_calls[0]        # ReAct: one action per step
        name, args = call["name"], call.get("args", {})
        observation = impls[name](args)
        trace.steps.append(ReactTraceStep(step_no, f"need {name}",
                                           name, args, observation))
        # TEACHING POINT: write the observation back, or it thrashes
        messages.append(("ai", f"{name}({args})"))
        messages.append(("tool", json.dumps(observation, default=str)))
    trace.terminated_reason = "step_budget_exhausted"
    return _finalise(trace)

callouts.text: The stub model only decides 'which tool, what args' — the control flow is this function's own code.
Skipping this line is the sim-react-thrash bug — the model re-asks and calls the same tool again.
Scored afterwards: the same (tool, args) pair seen twice is thrashing — wasted cost, made visible.

slides.notes: Trace one full pass on the board before revealing this: thought, action, observation, repeat. Point out there is no langgraph import anywhere in this function — that absence is the whole teaching point of building it explicit first.

slides.title: Plan-and-Execute: the inspectable plan

callouts.text: A structured, loggable Pydantic model — not prose buried in a chat reply.
Pure function: a refund/fraud/override step, or a plan over 5 steps, flags for a human — no model call.
plan_node logs the plan and the gate decision before a single step runs — the enterprise control point.

slides.notes: Point at plan_approval_gate and say: this is a pure function with no model call in it — that is deliberate, so the gate decision is itself auditable and testable without a live model. log_plan runs BEFORE the while loop that executes steps; that ordering is the whole enterprise argument.

slides.title: Reflection: bounded and concrete

callouts.text: Four checkable criteria, not 'make it better' — vague criteria add cost with no measurable gain.
MAX_REFLECTIONS = 2 — the loop always returns, even on best-effort, Module 1's discipline again.
Called only on refund/compliance drafts, never on 'where is my order'.

slides.notes: Read CRITERIA aloud — it is the example of 'concrete and checkable' the module keeps promising. Ask what would go wrong if criteria were just 'make it more helpful'; the answer is the code-review exercise coming up in a few slides.

slides.title: Six mistakes that inflate the bill

bullets.text: Because it is the tutorial pattern — the primary cause of runaway agent bills.
Plan-and-Execute with no way to recover when an observation invalidates the plan.
Critique-and-revise loops that run indefinitely.
'Make it better' adds cost with no measurable quality gain.
Shipping a pattern choice without a cost/latency/quality comparison on the eval set.
Plan-and-Execute's main enterprise benefit is thrown away if the plan is never surfaced or logged.

slides.notes: Mistake 1 is the one the room is most at risk of making themselves this afternoon in Lab 2 — say that directly. Ask which mistake the Saudi telecom case study (next slide) is really about before you reveal it: it is 1 and 5 together.

slides.title: Case study: an 18x telecom cost overrun
slides.scenario: A national telecom deployed a ReAct support agent for billing and plan questions. It handled everything — including the 70% of contacts that were simple balance checks — with full step-by-step reasoning. The billing forecast assumed roughly 0.03 SAR per contact against 45,000 contacts a day.
slides.challenge: Actuals came in near 0.55 SAR per contact — an 18x overrun that turned a cost-saving project into a budget crisis within one month. The team had to cut cost without losing the ability to handle genuinely complex contacts, with no downtime, the same tools and model gateway, and a defensible per-intent cost model for finance.
slides.solution: Intent triage first: route the 70% routine intents to a fixed, 2-step Plan-and-Execute flow; keep ReAct only for the long tail; add a Reflection gate solely on billing-adjustment outputs. Measured per-intent cost on a day's contacts before rollout. Blended cost came back under forecast, with the expensive pattern reserved for where it earns its keep.

slides.title: Five-question recap

bullets.text: One-line definition of ReAct? Interleave reasoning and acting until done.
Plan-and-Execute's main enterprise benefit beyond cost? An inspectable, approvable plan.
When should you not use Reflection? Low-stakes, easily reversible outputs.
Why does ReAct cost grow super-linearly with steps? Each step re-sends the growing history.
Name two ReAct failure modes. Thrashing and premature answering (also context bloat).

slides.title: Day 1 in one line
points: An agent is a bounded state machine — steps, cost and wall-clock time, checked in code, not hoped for in a prompt.
Chain vs agent is a control-flow choice; most production systems are mostly chain with agentic islands.
ReAct, Plan-and-Execute and Reflection are not competitors — they compose, and the composition is a cost decision.
You built the loop and all three reasoning patterns today. Tomorrow they get real tools.
